topics.title: Pattern overview
topics.summary: Prototype copies an already configured object without requiring its caller to know the object's concrete class. Worked example: Duplicate mixed presentation cues with independent edits. Each concrete cue implements clone with its own copy constructor. Value-owned strings and vectors give independent editable state, while unique_ptr states ownership of each new polymorphic object.

blocks.title: Learning objectives
items: Copy through a base interface while preserving concrete behavior.
State which data a clone owns and which resources may remain shared.
Verify independence by editing and destroying the original.

blocks.text: The base interface declares a virtual clone operation. Each concrete implementation creates its own concrete type using the current object as the source of values. The caller invokes clone through the base interface and receives a new object. A registry can hold named prototypes for reuse, but the registry is optional. The copy policy must say which data becomes independent and which resources, if any, remain shared.

cards.question: What problem does Prototype address?
cards.answer: Prototype copies an already configured object without requiring its caller to know the object's concrete class. Worked example: Duplicate mixed presentation cues with independent edits. Each concrete cue implements clone with its own copy constructor. Value-owned strings and vectors give independent editable state, while unique_ptr states ownership of each new polymorphic object.

cards.question: What is Prototype?
cards.answer: A pattern in which an existing object creates a new object by copying its own state through a common operation.

cards.question: What is Object slicing?
cards.answer: Losing the derived part when a derived object is copied into a base value.

cards.question: What is Deep copy?
cards.answer: A copy that duplicates owned contents to the independence depth required by the application.

cards.question: What is Shallow copy?
cards.answer: A copy that duplicates handles while retaining some shared underlying objects.

cards.question: Why is copying the unique_ptr address into another owning handle not cloning?
cards.answer: Both handles would own the same object, leading to double deletion. clone must create a distinct object with the promised copied state.

cards.question: Is a prototype registry required for the cue example?
cards.answer: No. The collection already supplies each source object. A registry becomes useful when callers need to look up configured prototypes by a key.

cards.question: Why is copying a unique_ptr member not a valid deep-copy implementation?
cards.answer: unique_ptr deliberately forbids copying ownership. The copy constructor must allocate a new string and copy the string value, giving each object its own release responsibility.

cards.question: Can clone return the same object under a new unique_ptr?
cards.answer: No. Two independent unique_ptr owners of one address would both delete it. A clone must be a distinct owned object under this contract.

cards.question: Why test destruction of the original before using the clone?
cards.answer: It checks independence of lifetime, not just equality of text. A shallow borrow may appear correct until the original goes away.

cards.question: Would a copied shared_ptr meet the independent-edit contract?
cards.answer: Not by itself. It would share one mutable object, so edits could leak between copies. Immutable sharing or copy-on-write would need an explicitly different design.

cards.question: What does copying through Cue& preserve that slicing Cue by value would lose?
cards.answer: Virtual clone selects the actual concrete kind. Base-value copying would not preserve derived state, and this abstract Cue cannot be instantiated as a value at all.

cards.question: Which part of ListCue makes its default copy sufficient?
cards.answer: vector<string> owns its elements as values. Copying it copies the strings; there are no borrowed element pointers that require a separate deep-copy loop.

cards.question: When is Prototype unnecessary?
cards.answer: When callers know the concrete type and ordinary value copying already expresses the requirement. Prototype helps copy through a common interface without naming every concrete kind.

topics.title: Duplicate cues without knowing their kinds
topics.summary: A presentation tool keeps a list of cues. A text cue has one name, such as Start. A list cue contains several names, such as Check and Begin. The user duplicates a group of cues and edits the first name in the copied list. The original group must remain unchanged. A cue name may not be empty, and a list must contain at least one name.

blocks.text: For a known TextCue, an ordinary copy is the simplest reasonable solution. C++ already knows how to copy a string member. No design pattern is needed for that case. The difficulty begins when a container stores owning handles to Cue and the duplication code cannot name each concrete type. The excerpt can copy a known object but does not solve copying an unknown derived object through its base interface.

discussion.question: After copying a presentation cue, should editing the copy change the original?
discussion.answer: No. The requirement is independent editing. Matching the initial text is only the first check; later edits and destruction of the original must not damage the copy.

topics.title: The limitation is lost concrete type information
topics.summary: A unique_ptr cannot be copied because copying the sole owner would give two owners responsibility for deleting one object. Copying Cue itself would not solve the problem either. Cue is abstract here, so it cannot be constructed. In a nonabstract hierarchy, copying only the base part can discard derived data and behavior, a problem called object slicing. Neither copying the handle nor copying only the base subobject means “make an independent object of the same actual kind.”

blocks.text: The Prototype pattern asks the existing object to create that copy. Cue declares a virtual clone operation returning a new owning Cue handle. TextCue and ListCue each know their own concrete type, so each can call its own copy constructor. The caller asks for a clone without deciding which constructor to invoke. Prototype is therefore about construction from an existing object’s state, not simply about any function named copy.

topics.title: What clone preserves
topics.summary: ListCue::clone calls make_unique<ListCue>(*this). this points at the current ListCue; *this refers to the whole current ListCue object. Inside a const member, that expression is a const reference suitable for copying. The explicitly defaulted copy constructor copies the vector member. Both concrete cue types declare their copy constructors this way, suppressing implicit object moves. Constructing from an rvalue therefore copies instead of emptying the source; moves of unique_ptr handles still transfer ownership without moving the cue object itself. Copying a vector of strings copies each string value, so the clone owns independent character data in the normal observable sense. Editing one list’s first name does not edit the other list’s name.

blocks.text: The clone’s type is still ListCue even though its returned owner is unique_ptr<Cue>. Later virtual calls to text and rename reach ListCue behavior. The new object has a different address but starts with the same public value. Equal value and shared identity are different ideas: two clocks can display the same time without being the same clock. The program checks both equal initial text and distinct object addresses.

During compilation, the compiler generates the appropriate memberwise copy constructor and checks the clone override signature. During execution, the actual cue chooses which clone override runs. Allocation creates new storage, construction copies the concrete object into it, and ownership returns to the caller. If copying fails, make_unique cleans up the allocated storage; the original remains owned by its existing handle.

topics.title: Copy depth is a design decision
topics.summary: A shallow copy copies a handle or address while keeping the same underlying resource. A deep copy makes an independent copy of owned contents, to the depth promised by the application. The words need a boundary. A vector of strings gives independent string values. A vector of shared_ptr<Image> would copy handles and share images unless the clone explicitly copied them. That may be correct if images are immutable and expensive, but it would not be correct for an independently editable image promise.

blocks.text: A unique_ptr member normally makes the containing type noncopyable until a copy operation is explicitly defined. The lab adds BoxCue with a unique_ptr<string>. Its copy constructor allocates a new string initialized from the original string. Simply returning make_unique<BoxCue>(*this) without that copy constructor would fail to compile. Replacing unique_ptr with shared_ptr just to silence the error would change ownership meaning and make edits visible through both handles.

Some resources should not be cloned at all. A live socket, open transaction, mutex, or hardware session has an identity that copying bytes cannot duplicate. A clone may copy configuration while opening a fresh session, share a documented immutable resource, or reject duplication. Cyclic object graphs need additional rules: a map from old objects to new objects can preserve internal relationships without infinite recursion. Do not promise a universal deep copy without defining where the copy stops.

topics.title: Keep the generic loop simple and the copy rules local
topics.summary: The loop over originals uses const auto& because each vector element is a unique_ptr and must not be copied. The reference borrows the owning handle; const prevents reseating that handle through this reference. It does not by itself make the pointed-to object const. clone is separately declared const to promise that cloning does not mutate the cue’s ordinary members. The arrow calls the operation on the object reached through the handle.

blocks.text: Each new owner goes into copies. push_back accepts the returned temporary owning handle by move. After the loop, originals and copies are separate owning collections. Destruction of either collection destroys only its own objects. The program renames the first entry of the copied ListCue and checks that the original text is still list:Check;Begin; while the copied text becomes list:Inspect;Begin;.

Prototype is useful for user duplication, reusable configured objects, and heterogeneous snapshots when copying has a clear domain meaning. A registry may keep named prototypes and return clones, but the registry is optional. If the concrete type is already known and ordinary value copying works, use it. If objects should have unique noncopyable identities, omit clone instead of adding a misleading operation. Maintaining a clone requires adding new fields to its copy policy as the type evolves, especially when members change from values to owning or shared handles.

blocks.title: Requirements
items: Duplicate cues through the Cue interface without selecting concrete constructors in the loop.
Preserve concrete behavior and initial public values.

blocks.text: Each concrete cue implements clone with its own copy constructor. Value-owned strings and vectors give independent editable state, while unique_ptr states ownership of each new polymorphic object.

blocks.title: Invariants
items: clone returns a new owner of the same concrete kind and equivalent initial value.
A successful rename preserves nonempty names.
Cloned editable contents do not alias originals.

blocks.text: Alternative: Ordinary copying is simpler for a container of one known value type. A variant of a closed set of cue types can also support value copying without a virtual clone. Prototype fits an extensible hierarchy whose concrete types are unknown to the duplication code.

Verification: main checks matching initial values for both cue kinds, a distinct text-cue address, independent list edits, rejected empty rename with preserved state, and rejected empty list construction. The lab additionally destroys an original before reading its cloned owned string. These checks do not define cloning of external resources or cyclic graphs.
Maintenance: Keep clone policy beside the concrete type. Review every newly added pointer-like member for whether it should copy deeply, share immutable state, or forbid cloning.

topics.title: Exercise 04.3: Diagnose a bug
topics.summary: A clone returns unique_ptr<Cue>(this), using a cast to remove const when needed. Explain the ownership failure even if the first printed text looks correct.

blocks.title: Hint
blocks.text: Count owners of the same address.

blocks.title: Explained answer
blocks.text: The result points to the original object rather than a new one. Both original and returned handles try to destroy it, producing double deletion and undefined behavior. Allocate a new concrete object using its copy constructor; never treat the source pointer as newly owned.

topics.title: Exercise 04.6: Justify a decision
topics.summary: A new cue refers to a 50 MB read-only image. Should every clone copy those bytes? Give a defensible sharing contract and the condition that would invalidate it.

blocks.title: Hint
blocks.text: Independence concerns permitted mutation, not necessarily identical storage layout.

blocks.title: Explained answer
blocks.text: Sharing an immutable image through shared_ptr<const Image> is reasonable when clones cannot mutate it and ownership keeps it alive. If users can edit image contents independently, sharing mutable storage violates the promise; use a deep copy or a carefully implemented copy-on-write policy. State which operations are allowed and who owns the lifetime.

discussion.question: A program stores only plain value records in vector<Record>. Another stores extensible derived cues behind unique_ptr<Cue>. Choose ordinary copying or Prototype and explain why.
discussion.answer: Copy the value vector normally in the first program. Use virtual clone for the open cue hierarchy when the copy site does not know concrete types. A variant is reasonable for a closed finite set of alternatives, but adding a new variant alternative requires updating the closed type definition.
discussion.hint: Is the complete concrete value type known at the copy site?

workshop.alternative: Ordinary copying is simpler for a container of one known value type. A variant of a closed set of cue types can also support value copying without a virtual clone. Prototype fits an extensible hierarchy whose concrete types are unknown to the duplication code.
workshop.design: Each concrete cue implements clone with its own copy constructor. Value-owned strings and vectors give independent editable state, while unique_ptr states ownership of each new polymorphic object.

A successful rename preserves nonempty names.
Cloned editable contents do not alias originals.
workshop.maintenance: Keep clone policy beside the concrete type. Review every newly added pointer-like member for whether it should copy deeply, share immutable state, or forbid cloning.
